Standard name: accumulated_total_gas_count
Definition (stored description): Cumulative equivalent-electron inventory of all gas species delivered by injection after plasma breakdown, summed across species.
Documentation (stored): This quantity is the cumulative equivalent-electron inventory of gas introduced into the plasma by injection after plasma breakdown. It combines all injected gas species into one total inventory. The total is defined by $$ N_{\mathrm{eq}}(t) = \sum_s z_s N_s(t) $$ where $N_{\mathrm{eq}}(t)$ is the accumulated equivalent-electron count, $s$ identifies an injected gas species, $N_s(t)$ is the cumulative number of particles of species $s$ delivered since plasma breakdown, and $z_s$ is the equivalent-electron contribution per particle; for an atomic species, $z_s$ is its atomic number, while for a molecule it is the sum of the atomic numbers of its constituent atoms. The quantity applies to all gas species and uses a cumulative sum over the post-breakdown injection history. It excludes gas introduced during prefill before plasma breakdown, instantaneous injection rates, and any single-species inventory such as [accumulated hydrogen count due to gas injection](name:accumulated_hydrogen_count_due_to_gas_injection). It is the post-breakdown counterpart of the prefill inventory [accumulated total prefill gas count](name:accumulated_total_prefill_gas_count); the two quantities differ by the injection phase they accumulate.
Stored unit: 1
Assigned physics domain: plant_systems

Standard name: area_of_diagnostic_aperture
Definition (stored description): Area of the diagnostic aperture opening in its own plane, excluding surrounding material and any transmission or detector-response weighting.
Documentation (stored): Area of diagnostic aperture The area is defined by: $$ A = \int_{\mathcal{S}} dS $$ where $A$ is the aperture area, $\mathcal{S}$ is the surface spanning the aperture opening, and $dS$ is an unsigned local area element. This quantity applies to one specified aperture, not an implicit sum over separate apertures. It excludes surrounding material and is not a transmission- or detector-response-weighted effective collecting area. It is distinct from the [detector-face surface area](name:surface_area_of_detector). For a circular aperture, $A = \pi r^2$, where $r$ is the [aperture radius](name:radius_of_diagnostic_aperture) and $\pi$ is the circle constant.

Standard name: coolant_mass_flow_rate
Definition (stored description): Coolant mass flow rate is the mass of coolant passing through a cooling loop, component, or port per unit time.
Documentation (stored): Coolant mass flow rate describes the mass throughput of coolant circulating through a cooling loop or passing through a component or port. The defining relation is: $$ \dot{m} = \frac{d m_{\mathrm{pass}}}{dt} $$ where $\dot{m}$ is the coolant mass flow rate, $m_{\mathrm{pass}}$ is the cumulative coolant mass passing through the selected flow cross section, and $t$ is elapsed time. The rate includes the complete coolant stream across that cross section; no sum over separate loops or components is implied. It is distinct from volumetric flow rate, local mass-flux density, and the rate of change of coolant inventory within a loop. For steady flow with negligible mechanical work and changes in kinetic and gravitational potential energy, the [coolant-absorbed power of a calorimetry component](name:coolant_absorbed_power_of_calorimetry_component) satisfies $P = \dot{m}(h_{\mathrm{out}}-h_{\mathrm{in}})$, where $P$ is the thermal power transferred to the coolant and $h_{\mathrm{out}}$ and $h_{\mathrm{in}}$ are its outlet and inlet specific enthalpies, respectively.
Stored unit: kg.s^-1
Assigned physics domain: mechanical_measurement_diagnostics

Standard name: derivative_of_volume_of_flux_surface_with_respect_to_poloidal_magnetic_flux_coordinate
Definition (stored description): Geometric rate of change of the cumulative volume enclosed by a nested magnetic flux surface as its signed poloidal flux coordinate varies.
Documentation (stored): This quantity is the geometric derivative of the cumulative volume enclosed by a nested magnetic flux surface with respect to its signed poloidal magnetic-flux coordinate. It is defined by $$ \frac{dV}{d\psi}=\frac{d}{d\psi}V(\psi) $$ where $V(\psi)$ is the volume enclosed by the flux surface labeled by $\psi$, $\psi$ is the signed poloidal magnetic-flux coordinate, and $d/d\psi$ denotes differentiation with respect to that coordinate. The quantity applies separately to each nested closed flux surface. The underlying volume is cumulative from the magnetic axis to the selected surface, so this derivative describes the change in enclosed volume along the flux coordinate rather than a local volume density, a shell volume, or a plasma-population-weighted quantity. It is the derivative of [volume enclosed by a flux surface](name:volume_of_flux_surface); integrating it between two flux-coordinate values gives the difference between the corresponding enclosed volumes. It is distinct from the derivative with respect to the toroidal flux coordinate, which is represented by [derivative of volume with respect to toroidal flux coordinate](name:derivative_of_volume_of_flux_surface_with_respect_to_toroidal_flux_coordinate). Sign convention: Positive when the enclosed volume increases in the direction of increasing signed poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$.

Assigned physics domain: equilibrium

Standard name: difference_of_vacuum_poloidal_current_function_and_initial_vacuum_poloidal_current_function
Definition (stored description): Signed change in the combined external-coil vacuum poloidal current function relative to its initial reference value, representing variation of the toroidal field multiplied by major radius.
Documentation (stored): The quantity is the signed difference between the present and initial values of the vacuum poloidal current function produced by external coil currents. It represents the change in the major-radius-weighted toroidal magnetic field in the axisymmetric current-free vacuum region. Let $F_{\rm vac}$ denote the [vacuum poloidal current function](name:vacuum_poloidal_current_function). Its change relative to the initial reference state is $$ \Delta F_{\rm vac}=F_{\rm vac}-F_{\rm vac,initial}=R B_{\phi,\rm vac}-R B_{\phi,\rm vac,initial} $$ where $\Delta F_{\rm vac}$ is the signed change, $F_{\rm vac}$ is the present external-coil vacuum poloidal current function, $F_{\rm vac,initial}$ is its value in the initial reference state, $R$ is major radius, and $B_{\phi,\rm vac}$ is the vacuum toroidal magnetic-field component in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. Here $\phi$ is toroidal angle and $Z$ is vertical height. The quantity uses the combined vacuum contribution from external coil currents and excludes plasma currents and induced currents in conducting structures. It is a difference from one initial reference value, not the absolute [vacuum poloidal current function](name:vacuum_poloidal_current_function); within an axisymmetric current-free region, it inherits the parent function's spatial constancy. Sign convention: Positive when the present value of $R B_{\phi,\rm vac}$ exceeds its initial reference value, with $B_{\phi,\rm vac}$ positive in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

Assigned physics domain: magnetic_field_systems

Standard name: effective_turn_count_of_passive_loop
Definition (stored description): Effective turn count of a passive loop is the signed number of equivalent windings assigned to a passive conducting loop for electromagnetic coupling. It weights the passive-loop current contribution and may be fractional for equivalent or homogenized loop elements.
Documentation (stored): Effective turn count of a passive loop is the signed number of equivalent windings assigned to a passive conducting loop for electromagnetic coupling. It may be fractional when the represented conductor is an equivalent or homogenized passive-loop element rather than a literal winding. The signed current-turn source strength represented by the passive loop is defined by: $$ \mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{loop}} = N_{\mathrm{eff}} I_{\mathrm{loop}} $$ where $\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{loop}}$ is the signed current-turn source strength of the passive loop, $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the effective turn count of the passive loop, and $I_{\mathrm{loop}}$ is the [current of the passive loop](name:current_of_passive_loop). This quantity applies to the represented passive loop or passive-loop element as one electromagnetic circuit contribution. It has no implicit aggregation over multiple passive loops; if several represented windings or conductor pieces are collapsed into one loop element, their net orientation and coupling are represented by the single algebraic value of $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$. It is distinct from the [current of the passive loop](name:current_of_passive_loop), which is multiplied by $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$, and from the [area of the passive loop](name:area_of_passive_loop), which describes conductor cross section. It is not a turn count for magnetic probes, coil conductor elements, toroidal-field coils, or magnetic field-line winding.

Standard name: electron_temperature_at_magnetic_axis
Definition (stored description): Temperature of electrons at the magnetic axis measures their local mean random kinetic energy per particle, excluding coherent electron flow.
Documentation (stored): Temperature of electron at magnetic axis The nonrelativistic defining relation is $$ T_{e,\mathrm{axis}} = \frac{2}{3}\left\langle E_{e,\mathrm{random}}\right\rangle_{\mathrm{axis}} $$ where $T_{e,\mathrm{axis}}$ is the electron temperature at the magnetic axis, $E_{e,\mathrm{random}}$ is the electron kinetic energy relative to the local mean electron flow, and the angle brackets denote a particle-number-weighted average over the local electron population. The subscript $\mathrm{axis}$ denotes evaluation at the magnetic axis. This quantity is a local value, not a volume average or a maximum over the plasma. It specializes [temperature at the magnetic axis](name:temperature_at_magnetic_axis) to the electron kinetic temperature, unlike [radiative temperature at the magnetic axis](name:radiative_temperature_at_magnetic_axis), which represents radiation brightness. It forms the numerator of the [ratio of on-axis to volume-averaged electron temperature](name:ratio_of_electron_temperature_at_magnetic_axis_to_volume_averaged_electron_temperature). That ratio expresses central temperature peaking relative to the electron-temperature volume average inside the last closed magnetic flux surface. The closed magnetic-field line about which nested toroidal magnetic flux surfaces are arranged. Where $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{p}}(R_{\mathrm{axis}}, Z_{\mathrm{axis}}) = 0$, $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{p}}$ is poloidal magnetic field; $R_{\mathrm{axis}}, Z_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the O-point inside the nested closed flux surfaces.

Standard name: elongation_of_flux_surface
Definition (stored description): Elongation of a flux surface is the ratio of its poloidal cross-section’s vertical extent to its radial extent, independent of overall size.
Documentation (stored): Elongation of flux surface In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the defining relation is: $$ \kappa = (Z_{\max} - Z_{\min})/(R_{\max} - R_{\min}) $$ where $\kappa$ is the elongation, $Z_{\max}$ and $Z_{\min}$ are the maximum and minimum vertical coordinates of the cross-section, and $R_{\max}$ and $R_{\min}$ are its maximum and minimum major radii. The quantity applies to an individual flux surface, not an average over nested surfaces. For an elliptical cross-section, it equals the ratio of the vertical to horizontal semi-axes; the extent-based definition does not require an ellipse. It is not restricted to the plasma boundary: evaluating it there gives the [elongation of the plasma boundary](name:elongation_of_plasma_boundary). The [derivative of elongation with respect to normalized minor radius](name:derivative_of_elongation_of_flux_surface_with_respect_to_normalized_minor_radius) describes how this ratio changes between neighboring surfaces, rather than the shape ratio itself. A surface formed by points sharing the same magnetic-flux label in a nested-flux-surface configuration. Where $\psi(R, Z) = \mathrm{const}$, $\psi$ is poloidal magnetic flux.

Standard name: faraday_angle
Definition (stored description): Faraday angle is the signed rotation of a probing beam's linear-polarization orientation accumulated as the beam propagates through magnetized plasma. It is sensitive to the line integral of electron density times the magnetic-field component along the beam path and is used to constrain equilibrium reconstruction.
Documentation (stored): Faraday angle is the signed rotation of the linear-polarization orientation of a probing electromagnetic wave induced by its passage through magnetized plasma. It is the variation of the polarization orientation accumulated between the beam's entry into and exit from the plasma. In the cold, weakly dispersive magnetoionic limit, the plasma-induced rotation is approximated by $$ \alpha = \frac{e^3\lambda^2}{8\pi^2\epsilon_0 m_e^2 c^3} \int_{\mathcal{L}} n_e(\ell) B_{\parallel}(\ell)\,d\ell $$ where $\alpha$ is the Faraday angle, $e$ is the elementary-charge magnitude, $\lambda$ is the vacuum probing wavelength, $\pi$ is the circle constant, $\epsilon_0$ is the vacuum permittivity, $m_e$ is the electron mass, and $c$ is the speed of light. The path $\mathcal{L}$ is the segment of the probing beam crossing the plasma, $\ell$ is position along that path, $n_e(\ell)$ is the local [electron number density](name:electron_density), and $B_{\parallel}(\ell)$ is the signed magnetic-field component along the beam-propagation direction. The quantity is the electron contribution accumulated along one probing-beam path through the plasma: its aggregation is a line integral along that path, not a local rotation rate, a flux-surface average, or an average or sum over beam paths. Rotation produced outside the plasma, including by optical or calibration elements, is excluded. The same physical angle may be realized either as a direct polarimetric observation or as the value calculated from a reconstructed equilibrium state along the same beam path; both denote this quantity, and their difference is a fit residual rather than another definition of it. Faraday angle describes rotation of the polarization plane, whereas [polarization ellipticity of a polarimeter beam](name:polarization_ellipticity_of_polarimeter_beam) describes the shape of the polarization ellipse through its axis ratio; the two quantities are distinct and not interchangeable. Sign convention: Positive when the polarization plane rotates according to the right-hand rule about the beam-propagation direction from its incident reference orientation.
Stored unit: rad
Assigned physics domain: equilibrium

Standard name: flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude
Definition (stored description): Flux-surface average of the inverse square of total equilibrium magnetic-field magnitude, a geometric coefficient in neoclassical and flux-surface-averaged transport relations.
Documentation (stored): Flux-surface-averaged inverse-square magnetic-field magnitude is a magnetic-geometry coefficient for equilibrium and neoclassical transport relations. It applies to the total equilibrium field on each closed nested magnetic flux surface. The coefficient is defined by $$ \langle B^{-2}\rangle = \oint B^{-2}\,dS/|\nabla\psi| \,/\, \oint dS/|\nabla\psi| $$ where $B$ is the total equilibrium magnetic-field magnitude, $B^{-2}$ is its local inverse square, $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic-flux label, $dS$ is the surface-area element, and $\nabla\psi$ is the gradient of the flux label. Both integrals extend over the closed magnetic flux surface labeled by $\psi$, and angle brackets denote the flux-surface average on that surface. All magnetic-field components contribute through the total magnitude; no individual component is selected. The definition requires nonzero field magnitude and finite surface integrals. This is the surface-averaged form of the [local inverse-square magnetic-field magnitude](name:inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude), rather than its pointwise value. Squaring and inversion precede averaging: the result is generally neither the inverse square of the [surface-averaged field magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_magnetic_field_magnitude) nor the reciprocal of the [surface-averaged squared field magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude). The flux-surface average is the average of a quantity over a closed magnetic flux surface, weighted by the inverse magnitude of the poloidal flux gradient. The inverse is the reciprocal of a quantity. The magnitude is the Euclidean norm of a vector quantity, or the modulus of a complex one. The square is a scalar quantity multiplied by itself, or a vector's dot product with itself.

Assigned physics domain: equilibrium

Standard name: flux_surface_averaged_major_radius
Definition (stored description): Major radius averaged over a complete closed magnetic flux surface gives the mean perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis.
Documentation (stored): Major radius is the [radius](name:radius) measured perpendicular to the toroidal symmetry axis. Its flux-surface-averaged value is a geometric equilibrium coefficient for each complete closed magnetic flux surface of a nested equilibrium. Its defining operator composition is $$\langle f\rangle = \oint f\,dS/|\nabla\psi| \,/\, \oint dS/|\nabla\psi|$$ where $\overline{R}(\psi)$ is this coefficient, $R$ is the pointwise [major radius](name:major_radius), $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux labeling the surface, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_\psi$ denotes the flux-surface average on that surface. This quantity is the averaged counterpart of pointwise major radius, not a volume average or the major radius evaluated at a selected point. It applies wherever the flux-surface average is well defined and finite. The reciprocal of this mean generally differs from the [flux-surface-averaged inverse of major radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_major_radius), because that sibling applies inversion before averaging. Standard name: forward_wave_phase_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna
Definition (stored description): Forward phase at an ion-cyclotron heating antenna is the relative phase angle of a module's forward radio-frequency power-wave phasor with respect to the corresponding phasor of the first module.
Documentation (stored): Forward wave phase of an ion-cyclotron heating antenna is the relative phase angle of the complex forward radio-frequency power-wave phasor of one selected antenna module with respect to the corresponding forward phasor of the first module. It denotes a single object: the module-to-module phasing of forward waves, not an absolute phase and not a forward-versus-reflected phase at one module. For selected module $j$, the quantity is defined by $$ \varphi_j^{\mathrm{fwd}} = \arg\!\left(a_j^{\mathrm{fwd}} \left(a_1^{\mathrm{fwd}}\right)^*\right) \pmod{2\pi} $$ where $\varphi_j^{\mathrm{fwd}}$ is the forward wave phase of module $j$, $j$ identifies the selected module, module $1$ is the first module, $a_j^{\mathrm{fwd}}$ and $a_1^{\mathrm{fwd}}$ are the complex forward power-wave phasors of modules $j$ and $1$, $*$ denotes complex conjugation, and $\arg$ extracts the phase angle. The phase is defined modulo $2\pi$ and is undefined if either phasor is zero. The scope is the forward wave of one selected module relative to the first module. It is not an absolute phase relative to a source or oscillator, and it is not averaged or summed over modules. For the first module itself the relative phase is zero whenever its phasor is nonzero. This is the forward-wave specialization of the [wave phase of the ion-cyclotron heating antenna](name:wave_phase_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna). Unlike the [reflected phase of the ion-cyclotron heating antenna](name:reflected_phase_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna), which compares the reflected and forward waves at one element, it compares forward waves across modules. It is distinct from the [wave phase of an antenna strap](name:wave_phase_of_antenna_strap), which refers to strap-level excitation. The [forward power of the ion-cyclotron heating antenna](name:forward_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna) is the power carried by the forward wave and carries no phase information; this phase carries no information on wave power. Sign convention: Positive when the selected module's forward-wave phasor leads the first module's phasor; for modules ordered toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame with basis $(\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})$, this phase progression corresponds to propagation in the $+\hat{\phi}$ direction under the negative-exponential temporal phasor convention.

Standard name: height_of_poloidal_field_coil

Standard name: initial_polarization_ellipticity_of_polarimeter_beam
Definition (stored description): Initial ellipticity of a polarimeter beam is the signed minor-to-major semiaxis ratio of its incident electric-field polarization ellipse before plasma entry.
Documentation (stored): Initial ellipticity of a polarimeter beam characterizes the shape and handedness of its incident electric-field polarization ellipse as part of the polarization state before plasma entry. For an incident polarization ellipse, the ellipticity is defined by $$ e_0 = \sigma_0 \frac{b_0}{a_0} $$ where $e_0$ is the initial polarization ellipticity, $a_0$ and $b_0$ are the major and minor semiaxis magnitudes of the incident electric-field polarization ellipse, and $\sigma_0$ is the handedness sign of the incident polarization state. The semiaxes satisfy $0 \le b_0 \le a_0$, so $|e_0| \le 1$; $e_0=0$ corresponds to linear polarization and $|e_0|=1$ to circular polarization. This quantity applies to one incident polarimeter-beam polarization state along a specified line of sight, with no aggregation across distinct beam paths. It is not the full initial polarization vector, does not describe the post-propagation state, and does not encode the ellipse orientation; the [Faraday angle](name:faraday_angle) describes that orientation's rotation. The initial ellipticity is the reference value for plasma-induced changes in ellipticity, including changes caused by Cotton–Mouton birefringence. The [polarization ellipticity of a polarimeter beam](name:polarization_ellipticity_of_polarimeter_beam) describes the corresponding ellipse shape after propagation through magnetized plasma. Sign convention: Positive when, in the right-handed beam-local basis $(\hat{e}_1,\hat{e}_2,\hat{k})$ with $\hat{k}$ along beam propagation, $\hat{e}_1$ along the major semiaxis, and $\hat{e}_2=\hat{k}\times\hat{e}_1$, the electric-field vector rotates from $+\hat{e}_1$ toward $+\hat{e}_2$ as time increases.

Standard name: launched_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna
Definition (stored description): Launched power of a lower-hybrid antenna is the net RF power coupled into the vacuum vessel toward the plasma, equal to the forward power minus the reflected power at the launching unit. The launching unit may be an antenna module, a single antenna, or the complete antenna set, for which the value is the sum over the constituent units.
Documentation (stored): Launched power of a lower-hybrid antenna is the nonnegative net RF power coupled from the launching structure into the vacuum vessel toward the plasma. It is the net-transfer component of the wave-power budget represented by [power of a lower-hybrid antenna](name:power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna). The launched power is defined by the balance: $$ P_\mathrm{launched} = P_\mathrm{forward} - P_\mathrm{reflected} $$ where $P_\mathrm{forward}$ is the [forward power of a lower-hybrid antenna](name:forward_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna) arriving at the antenna input reference plane from the transmission line, $P_\mathrm{reflected}$ is the [reflected power of a lower-hybrid antenna](name:reflected_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna) returning toward the transmission line, and $P_\mathrm{launched}$ is the net power entering the vacuum vessel. The launching unit may be an antenna module, a single antenna, or the complete lower-hybrid antenna set. The quantity is extensive, so the launched power of a composite unit is the sum of the launched powers of its constituent units. Launched power excludes the reflected contribution and is distinct from forward power, which includes the portion subsequently reflected. It denotes the net power delivered across the launching aperture into the vessel, not the generator output on the transmission-line side of the reference plane, and it does not by itself resolve where the power is subsequently deposited within the plasma. The [toroidal-mode-resolved launched power](name:launched_power_per_toroidal_mode_of_lower_hybrid_antenna) and the [jointly toroidal- and poloidal-mode-resolved launched power](name:launched_power_per_toroidal_and_poloidal_mode_number_of_lower_hybrid_antenna) are distributions of this same quantity over refractive-index intervals; integrating them over those intervals recovers the launched power of the corresponding antenna row.

Standard name: loop_voltage_at_plasma_boundary
Definition (stored description): Loop voltage at the plasma boundary is the electromotive force around a closed toroidal loop that provides the inductive drive for ohmic plasma current.
Documentation (stored): Loop voltage at plasma boundary The voltage is defined by the electric-field circulation: $$ V_{\mathrm{loop}} = \oint_C \mathbf{E}\cdot d\mathbf{l} $$ where $V_{\mathrm{loop}}$ is the boundary loop voltage, $C$ is the closed toroidal loop at the plasma boundary, $\mathbf{E}$ is the electric field, and $d\mathbf{l}$ is the directed line element along the loop. The total includes inductive contributions from both external sources and plasma currents. In contrast, [external loop voltage](name:external_loop_voltage) denotes only the contribution from changing externally generated linked magnetic flux. The inductive electric field provides the drive for [current due to ohmic current drive](name:current_due_to_ohmic_current_drive); the loop voltage is not an electrostatic potential difference between two points. Sign convention: Positive when the electric-field circulation is directed along increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counterclockwise viewed from above) in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. The last closed magnetic flux surface: the outermost flux surface on which field lines close on themselves, bounding the confined plasma. Where $\psi = \psi_{\mathrm{LCFS}}$, $\psi$ is poloidal magnetic flux; $\psi_{\mathrm{LCFS}}$ is its value on the last closed flux surface.

Together with [upper photon energy](name:upper_photon_energy), this bound specifies the spectral window. Standard name: minimum_over_flux_surface_magnetic_field_magnitude
Definition (stored description): Smallest total magnetic-field strength attained along a specified nested magnetic flux surface, using the field magnitude rather than a signed component.
Documentation (stored): The minimum magnetic-field magnitude is the smallest total field strength attained anywhere on a specified nested magnetic flux surface. It is sign-invariant because it uses the modulus of the magnetic-field vector rather than a signed component. For a surface labeled by the magnetic-flux coordinate $\psi$, the quantity is defined by $$ B_{\min}(\psi) = \min_{\mathbf{x} \in S(\psi)} \left|\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x})\right| $$ where $B_{\min}(\psi)$ is the minimum magnetic-field magnitude, $\mathbf{x}$ is a position on the surface, $S(\psi)$ is the set of positions belonging to the flux surface labeled by $\psi$, and $\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x})$ is the total magnetic-field vector at that position. The minimum is taken over all positions on each nested magnetic flux surface and includes the complete equilibrium field, including its poloidal and toroidal contributions. It is not a signed component minimum, a flux-surface average, or a minimum taken across multiple flux surfaces. Unlike the [flux-surface-averaged inverse square of magnetic-field magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude), this quantity reduces the field magnitude itself by a pointwise minimum rather than averaging its reciprocal square.

Standard name: minimum_safety_factor
Definition (stored description): Signed safety-factor value on the closed magnetic flux surface where the magnitude of field-line winding is smallest, distinct from that surface’s location.
Documentation (stored): The minimum safety factor is the signed field-line winding number evaluated on the nested closed magnetic flux surface where the magnitude of the safety factor is smallest. It represents the extremal value of the safety-factor function within the confined closed-surface domain. The minimizing value is defined by $$ q_{\min} = q(\rho_\ast), \qquad \rho_\ast \in \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{0 \leq \rho \leq 1} |q(\rho)| $$ where $q(\rho)$ is the signed [safety factor](name:safety_factor) on the flux surface labeled by $\rho$, $\rho_\ast$ is the label of a surface at which the magnitude $|q(\rho)|$ is minimized, and $q_{\min}$ is the signed value evaluated there. The label $\rho$ is a monotonic flux-surface coordinate whose endpoints denote the magnetic axis and the last closed flux surface. In flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, $\theta$ is the poloidal angle and $\phi$ is the toroidal angle of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. The extremum is taken over all nested closed magnetic flux surfaces and is neither a flux-surface average nor a sum. The location-defining quantity is separate: poloidal magnetic flux at minimum safety factor identifies the corresponding surface, while this quantity reports only the signed safety factor. It is also distinct from a safety factor evaluated at a prescribed locus, such as the magnetic axis. Sign convention: Positive when the toroidal angle advance of a magnetic field line is in the direction of increasing $\phi$ as the poloidal angle $\theta$ increases.

Standard name: normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate
Definition (stored description): Normalized poloidal flux coordinate labels nested magnetic surfaces by the square root of the poloidal-flux fraction between the magnetic axis and the last closed flux surface. It ranges from zero at the magnetic axis to one at that surface.
Documentation (stored): Normalized poloidal flux coordinate. The associated linear normalized poloidal-flux fraction is $$ \psi_{\mathrm{N}} = \frac{\psi - \psi_{\mathrm{axis}}}{\psi_{\mathrm{b}} - \psi_{\mathrm{axis}}} $$ where $\psi_{\mathrm{N}}$ is the linear normalized poloidal-flux fraction, $\psi$ is the [poloidal magnetic flux at the flux surface](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_flux_surface) being labeled, $\psi_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the [poloidal magnetic flux at the magnetic axis](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis), and $\psi_{\mathrm{b}}$ is the [poloidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary), with the reference boundary being the last closed flux surface. The axis and boundary reference fluxes must differ. The coordinate is the square-root form, $\rho_{\mathrm{pol,norm}} = \sqrt{\psi_{\mathrm{N}}}$, where $\rho_{\mathrm{pol,norm}}$ denotes this normalized poloidal flux coordinate. Within nested closed magnetic surfaces from the magnetic axis to the last closed flux surface, the coordinate increases from zero to one and is constant on each surface. At a local point it labels the surface passing through that point; for a line-of-sight locus, the assigned coordinate is the minimum along the line, not a path average, endpoint value, or integral. It is a flux-surface label, not a geometric minor-radius fraction, physical distance, flux-surface average, or volume average. Locus-specific forms retain this coordinate while selecting a particular location: [normalized poloidal flux coordinate at measurement position](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_at_reflectometer_cutoff_position) gives the local value or, for a line-of-sight locus, the minimum along the line; [normalized poloidal flux coordinate at reflectometer cutoff position](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_at_reflectometer_cutoff_position) evaluates it at the cutoff; [normalized poloidal flux coordinate of plasma boundary](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary) evaluates it at the specified boundary; and [normalized poloidal flux coordinate at minimum absolute safety factor](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_at_minimum_absolute_safety_factor) locates the surface where the magnitude of the [safety factor](name:safety_factor) is smallest, rather than giving that minimum value. The [normalized poloidal flux coordinate of pedestal](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_pedestal) uses the linear flux fraction, not this square-root parameterization. The linear and square-root values share surface ordering but are not numerically interchangeable. This poloidal-flux label is distinct from the [normalized toroidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate), which is based on toroidal rather than poloidal flux. $$\psi_{\mathrm{N}} = (\psi - \psi_{\mathrm{axis}})/(\psi_{\mathrm{b}} - \psi_{\mathrm{axis}})$$

Standard name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_of_flux_loop
Definition (stored description): Poloidal magnetic flux of an individual flux loop is the measured, signed vertical-field integral over a horizontal disk centered on the toroidal symmetry axis.
Documentation (stored): Poloidal magnetic flux of an individual flux loop is the signed poloidal flux represented by that loop's measured value. For an axisymmetric magnetic field, its defining relation is $$ \Phi_{\mathrm{p}} = 2\pi \int_0^{R_\ell} B_Z(R', Z_\ell)\,R'\,dR' $$ where $\Phi_{\mathrm{p}}$ is the poloidal magnetic flux, $B_Z$ is the vertical magnetic-field component, and $R'$ is the integration radius. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; $R_\ell$ and $Z_\ell$ specify the evaluation location at the flux loop. The integration disk has its positive normal toward increasing $Z$. This is the loop-specific value of [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux), not a sum or average over multiple loops. It represents an integrated flux rather than a local magnetic-field value and is distinct from [toroidal magnetic flux](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux). Sign convention: Positive when the net magnetic flux through the integration disk is directed toward increasing $Z$.

Standard name: radial_coordinate_at_inboard_midplane
Definition (stored description): Major-radius coordinate of a magnetic flux surface at its inboard midplane intersection, locating the high-field-side point relative to the toroidal symmetry axis.
Documentation (stored): This quantity is the major-radius coordinate of the point where a magnetic flux surface intersects the inboard midplane, identifying the high-field-side location of that surface relative to the toroidal symmetry axis. It is a locus-specific form of the [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate). For a magnetic flux surface $\mathcal{S}$, the inboard-midplane radial coordinate is defined by $$ R_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathcal{S}) = R\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathcal{S})\right) $$ where $R_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathcal{S})$ is the quantity defined here, $R(\mathbf{x})$ is the major-radius coordinate of spatial position $\mathbf{x}$, $\mathcal{S}$ is the specified magnetic flux surface, and $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathcal{S})$ is its inboard midplane intersection. The coordinates are expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The scope is one coordinate value for each specified magnetic flux surface at its inboard, high-field-side midplane intersection. It is not a flux-surface average, a poloidal or toroidal average, or the corresponding outboard-midplane coordinate; the latter is represented by [radial coordinate at outboard midplane](name:radial_coordinate_at_outboard_midplane). Unlike [radial magnetic field](name:radial_magnetic_field), this quantity describes the location of a surface and not a magnetic-field component. This quantity specializes [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate) by fixing the evaluation locus to the inboard midplane. Comparing it with the outboard-midplane value characterizes the horizontal extent and radial placement of the same magnetic flux surface.

Standard name: spectral_bremsstrahlung_photon_radiance
Definition (stored description): Spectral bremsstrahlung photon radiance is the free-free continuum photon rate per projected area, viewing solid angle, and wavelength interval, evaluated at the spectrum center.
Documentation (stored): Spectral bremsstrahlung photon radiance describes free-free plasma emission as a directional photon-number rate resolved by projected area, solid angle, and wavelength. It denotes the continuum background level evaluated at the spectrum's central wavelength. Its photon-count definition is $$ L_{\gamma}(\lambda_c) = \left.\frac{\mathrm{d}^4 N_{\gamma}}{\mathrm{d}t\,\mathrm{d}A_{\perp}\,\mathrm{d}\Omega\,\mathrm{d}\lambda}\right|_{\lambda=\lambda_c} $$ where $L_{\gamma}$ is the spectral bremsstrahlung photon radiance, $N_{\gamma}$ is the number of bremsstrahlung photons, $t$ is time, $A_{\perp}$ is the area projected perpendicular to the viewing direction, $\Omega$ is the solid angle about that direction, $\lambda$ is wavelength, and $\lambda_c$ is the spectrum's central wavelength. This quantity is the bremsstrahlung continuum contribution to [spectral photon radiance](name:spectral_photon_radiance) along the viewing direction, rather than a local volumetric emissivity or an energy radiance. It excludes discrete line emission and differs from [photon radiance at a spectral line](name:photon_radiance_at_spectral_line), which is integrated over the wavelength interval of an identified transition. Integrating the spectral continuum over a specified wavelength interval gives the corresponding band-integrated continuum photon radiance. The central-wavelength value defined here is not itself a wavelength integral.

Standard name: spectral_calibration_factor_at_line_of_sight
Definition (stored description): Wavelength-specific interferometric conversion coefficient that converts a signed phase change along a line of sight into electron column density.
Documentation (stored): The spectral calibration factor is the wavelength-specific proportionality that maps an interferometric phase change along one line of sight to the electron column density on that optical path. The conversion is defined by $$ N_{e,\mathrm{line}} = K_{\mathrm{spec}}\,\Delta\varphi $$ where $N_{e,\mathrm{line}}$ is the [line-integrated electron number density](name:line_integrated_electron_number_density), $K_{\mathrm{spec}}$ is this spectral calibration factor, and $\Delta\varphi$ is the signed interferometric phase change. The factor applies to the complete electron-density integral along the associated line of sight and to its corresponding probing wavelength. It represents the electron contribution only and is not a local density, a line-averaged density, or an optical phase itself. Applying this factor produces the line-integrated electron number density; dividing that result by the optical chord length gives [line-averaged electron density](name:line_averaged_electron_density). The associated wavelength is the spectral parameter of the probing electromagnetic wave, related to [wavelength of wave beam](name:wavelength_of_wave_beam).

Standard name: spectral_rate_of_spectrometer_channel
Definition (stored description): Detected photoelectron rate assigned to each wavelength pixel of a spectrometer channel after electronic gain compensation and relative calibration, but before absolute radiometric calibration.
Documentation (stored): This quantity is the spectrally resolved detection rate of photoelectrons produced by a spectrometer channel. It represents the channel response at an individual wavelength pixel rather than an absolutely calibrated optical emission quantity. The rate for wavelength pixel $p$ is defined by $$ R_p = \frac{dN_{\mathrm{pe},p}}{dt} $$ where $R_p$ is the detected photoelectron rate for pixel $p$, $N_{\mathrm{pe},p}$ is the detected photoelectron count assigned to that pixel, and $t$ is time. The quantity applies separately to each wavelength pixel of the spectrometer channel, with electronic gain compensation and relative channel calibration applied. Standard name: thermal_electron_pressure_at_post_sawtooth_crash
Definition (stored description): Pressure of thermal electrons at the post-sawtooth-crash locus is the isotropic stress from random electron motion in the plasma edge and scrape-off layer.
Documentation (stored): Pressure of electron at post sawtooth crash The pressure is defined by the isotropic second central velocity moment: $$ p_e = \frac{m_e}{3}\int |\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}_e|^2 f_{e,\mathrm{th}}(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v $$ where $p_e$ is the thermal electron pressure, $m_e$ is the electron mass, $\mathbf{v}$ is electron velocity, $\mathbf{u}_e$ is the mean velocity of the thermal electron population, $f_{e,\mathrm{th}}$ is its velocity distribution whose integral equals the thermal-electron number density, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element. The integral extends over velocity space for the thermal population only. This quantity includes only thermal electrons, not a sum over plasma species. It excludes fast and other nonthermal electron contributions, ion pressure, and stress from directed bulk motion. It is an isotropic pressure rather than a field-parallel or field-perpendicular tensor component. It supplies the electron contribution to [thermal plasma pressure](name:thermal_plasma_pressure), which also includes thermal-ion contributions. At the same evaluation locus, [total electron pressure](name:total_electron_pressure) is the additive combination of this thermal contribution and any nonthermal electron pressure.

Standard name: toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe
Definition (stored description): The toroidal angle of a toroidal magnetic-field probe is the signed azimuthal orientation of the probe sensitive-axis normal projected onto the horizontal plane, measured from +R toward increasing φ in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame. Opposite projected normals are folded into the same principal orientation.
Documentation (stored): The toroidal angle of a toroidal magnetic-field probe is the signed azimuthal orientation of the probe sensitive-axis normal after projection onto the horizontal plane spanned by $\hat R$ and $\hat\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. Its zero direction is the outward radial direction, and the projected normal is treated as an orientation axis rather than a directed vector. The angle is defined by the two-argument arctangent of the horizontal normal components, folded modulo $\pi$ into the principal interval $(-\pi/2, \pi/2]$: $$ \alpha_\phi = \mathcal{F}_{(-\pi/2,\pi/2]}\!\left(\operatorname{atan2}(n_\phi,n_R)\right) $$ where $\alpha_\phi$ is this toroidal angle, $n_R$ and $n_\phi$ are the radial and toroidal scalar components of the normalized probe sensitive-axis normal vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and $\mathcal{F}_{(-\pi/2,\pi/2]}(\beta)$ denotes the representative of an angle $\beta$ after adding an integer multiple of $\pi$ that lies in $(-\pi/2, \pi/2]$. This quantity applies only to toroidal magnetic-field probes and is defined separately for each probe. It describes sensor orientation, not the [toroidal angle](name:toroidal_angle) that locates a point and not the probe position; no aggregation over multiple probes is implied. With the modulo-$\pi$ folding, projections parallel or antiparallel to $+\hat R$ have $\alpha_\phi=0$, and projections parallel or antiparallel to $+\hat\phi$ have the principal value $\alpha_\phi=\pi/2$. Together with the [poloidal angle of a toroidal magnetic-field probe](name:poloidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe), it specifies the orientation of the same sensitive-axis normal; it is the toroidal-field-probe-specific counterpart of the [toroidal angle of a magnetic-field probe](name:toroidal_angle_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe). Sign convention: Positive when the horizontal orientation is tilted from the radial basis line toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Standard name: toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_field
Definition (stored description): Toroidal magnetic field at the reference major radius generated by currents outside the plasma, with its directional sign retained and plasma-current contributions excluded.
Documentation (stored): Toroidal magnetic field at the reference major radius is the signed toroidal projection of the externally generated [magnetic induction](name:magnetic_field). It specifies the nominal vacuum field with plasma-current contributions omitted. The reference value is defined by projection: $$ B_0 = B_{\phi,\mathrm{vac}}(R_0) = \left.\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{vac}}\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}\right|_{R=R_0} $$ where $B_0$ is the reference vacuum toroidal field, $B_{\phi,\mathrm{vac}}$ is the local vacuum toroidal component, $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{vac}}$ is the [vacuum magnetic-field vector](name:vacuum_magnetic_field), and $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ is the unit vector toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius, $Z$ is vertical height, and $R_0$ is the specified reference major radius. This quantity is a component evaluated at the reference radius, not a field magnitude or spatial average. It differs from the total toroidal magnetic field by excluding plasma-generated contributions; the reference radius is not implicitly the magnetic-axis radius. In an axisymmetric current-free region, the [vacuum poloidal current function](name:vacuum_poloidal_current_function) $F_{\mathrm{vac}}$ satisfies $F_{\mathrm{vac}}=R B_{\phi,\mathrm{vac}}=R_0B_0$. This reference field also supplies the field scale for the [toroidal flux coordinate](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate) and associated current-density normalizations. Sign convention: Positive when the vacuum magnetic-field projection points toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, counterclockwise when viewed from above.

Standard name: total_external_heating_power
Definition (stored description): Total non-inductive power coupled from external neutral-beam and radio-frequency heating systems to the plasma, summed over auxiliary sources and excluding Ohmic heating.
Documentation (stored): Total external heating power is the aggregate non-inductive power coupled to the plasma by auxiliary heating systems. It includes neutral-beam injection and electron-cyclotron, ion-cyclotron, and lower-hybrid systems, while excluding power associated with Ohmic induction. The defining aggregate relation is $$ P_{\mathrm{ext}} = \sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{aux}}} P_s $$ where $P_{\mathrm{ext}}$ is the total external heating power, $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{aux}}$ is the set of included auxiliary heating systems, and $P_s$ is the power coupled to the plasma by auxiliary source $s$. The quantity applies to the whole plasma and is summed over all included auxiliary sources rather than resolved by source, species, or spatial region. It represents external power input that may contribute to both plasma heating and non-inductive current drive; it is distinct from Ohmic heating and from generator power that is not coupled to the plasma. Source-specific contributions include [total power due to electron-cyclotron heating](name:total_power_due_to_electron_cyclotron_heating), [total power due to ion-cyclotron heating](name:total_power_due_to_ion_cyclotron_heating), and power absorbed from a neutral-beam injector, whose aggregate forms contribute to the sum.

Standard name: total_power_due_to_ohmic_dissipation
Definition (stored description): Total ohmic power deposited in the plasma during a disruption by irreversible resistive heating from the plasma current.
Documentation (stored): Total ohmic power is the rate of irreversible electrical-energy conversion into heat within the plasma, caused by resistive dissipation of the plasma current. During a disruption, it contributes to plasma heating through the thermal and current quench phases. For the plasma domain, the ohmic power is defined by $$ P_{\rm ohm} = \int_{V_{\rm p}} \eta\,\lvert\mathbf{J}\rvert^2\,dV $$ where $P_{\rm ohm}$ is the total plasma ohmic power, $V_{\rm p}$ is the plasma volume, $\eta$ is the plasma electrical resistivity, $\mathbf{J}$ is the plasma current-density vector, and $dV$ is a volume element. The quantity aggregates resistive heating over the full plasma volume as a single deposited power, rather than denoting only the halo-region contribution. It excludes non-ohmic plasma heating and Joule heating in solid structures. In contrast, [wall ohmic-dissipation power](name:power_at_wall_due_to_ohmic_dissipation) aggregates resistive heating within conducting wall and vessel structures, not the plasma. The effective [plasma resistance](name:plasma_resistance), $R_{\rm p}$, relates this power to the total plasma current $I_{\rm p}$ through $P_{\rm ohm}=I_{\rm p}^{2}R_{\rm p}$. Reversible changes in magnetic-field energy are not included in this dissipated power. The [accumulated ohmic energy](name:accumulated_energy_due_to_ohmic_dissipation) is the time integral of this power over the accumulation interval.

Documentation (stored): Upper-bound photon energy is the maximum photon energy included in a specified X-ray emission or detection band. It defines the high-energy cutoff of that band. The photon-energy interval defined by this upper boundary and its lower boundary satisfies: $$ E_{\gamma,\min} \le E_{\gamma} \le E_{\gamma,\max} $$ where $E_{\gamma}$ is [photon energy](name:photon_energy), $E_{\gamma,\min}$ is the [lower-bound photon energy](name:lower_bound_photon_energy), and $E_{\gamma,\max}$ is the upper-bound photon energy defined here. For hard X-ray emissivity specified over an energy band common to all contributing channels, this bound is the shared upper integration limit. For detection, it delimits the selected photon-acceptance interval. It is distinct from a band-center energy, the band width, and the detector response within the band; it does not specify the maximum energy of the entire emitted photon population.

Standard name: vertical_coordinate_of_measurement_position
Definition (stored description): Vertical coordinate of a measurement position, specifying its signed location along the vertical direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
Documentation (stored): The vertical coordinate of a measurement position is its signed coordinate along the vertical direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The vertical direction is parallel to the toroidal symmetry axis. The coordinate is the projection of the position vector onto the vertical direction: $$ Z = \mathbf{x}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{z}} $$ Here $Z$ is the vertical coordinate, $\mathbf{x}$ is the position vector from the coordinate origin to the measurement position, and $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ is the unit vector along the symmetry axis in the positive vertical direction. In the frame $(R, \phi, Z)$, $R$ is major radius measured from the symmetry axis, and $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counterclockwise when viewed from above the positive vertical direction. This is one coordinate component of the represented measurement position, not the complete position or a measured physical value. Each value pertains to the position under consideration rather than aggregating coordinates over a population of positions. Its corresponding major-radius component is the [radial coordinate of the measurement position](name:radial_coordinate_of_measurement_position). Sign convention: Positive when the displacement from the coordinate origin to the measurement position points in the direction of increasing $Z$.

Standard name: vertical_outline_of_limiter_tile
Definition (stored description): Signed vertical (Z) coordinate of each point on a limiter-tile boundary contour in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
Documentation (stored): The vertical outline of a limiter tile gives the signed vertical coordinate of each point on the tile’s geometric boundary contour. Here, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The quantity applies pointwise to the irregular outline of one limiter tile in its poloidal cross section. Standard name: wave_phase_of_wave_beam
Definition (stored description): Wave phase of the wave beam is the angular argument of the probing-wave envelope; when referenced to launch, it is the envelope phase offset from the launch phase.
Documentation (stored): The wave phase is the angular argument of the complex probing-wave envelope at the wave-beam locus. It is defined relative to a phase origin; when the origin is the launch phase, the value is a signed phase difference rather than an absolute phase with a universal zero. For a launch-referenced value, the phase difference is: $$ \varphi = \varphi_{\mathrm{env}} - \varphi_{\mathrm{launch}} \pmod{2\pi} $$ where $\varphi$ is the launch-referenced phase difference, represented by difference of wave phase and launched wave phase of the wave beam; $\varphi_{\mathrm{env}}$ is the envelope phase at the wave-beam locus; and $\varphi_{\mathrm{launch}}$ is the launched wave phase. The phases use the same phase convention, and $2\pi$ is one full phase revolution. This quantity is the envelope phase, not the carrier oscillation phase. Values differing by an integer number of full revolutions represent the same phase; an unwrapped phase selects a continuous branch, and fringe-jump correction changes that representation without changing the phase modulo one revolution. Sign convention: Positive when the envelope phase at the wave-beam locus advances counterclockwise relative to the launch phase, using the positive-time-exponent phasor convention.
